extraction.name: OpenBookQA
extraction.description: OpenBookQA is a question answering dataset modeled after open book exams for assessing human understanding of a subject. It consists of about 5,957 multiple-choice elementary-level science questions (4,957 train, 500 dev, 500 test), probing understanding of a small 'book' of 1,326 core science facts and their application to novel situations. Answering the questions requires combining facts from the open book with broad common knowledge. Human performance is close to 92%, while state-of-the-art pre-trained QA methods perform poorly.
extraction.creator: Todor Mihaylov, Peter Clark, Tushar Khot, Ashish Sabharwal
extraction.citeAs: Mihaylov, T., Clark, P., Khot, T., & Sabharwal, A. (2018). Can a Suit of Armor Conduct Electricity? A New Dataset for Open Book Question Answering. arXiv:1809.02789.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The dataset was created via a multi-stage crowdsourcing and partial expert filtering process. Crowd-workers from Amazon Mechanical Turk (North America, 'masters' qualification) were shown a random science fact from F, asked to think of a second common fact k that combined with f produces a new valid assertion, then converted it into a 4-way multiple-choice question. The system verified uniformity checks, fed the question to an IR solver and word-association solver to verify hardness, and then 5 new crowd-workers answered the question; if at least 4/5 answered correctly, it was deemed answerable. Answer choices were shuffled to avoid bias. Dev and Test splits were further filtered by an in-house expert.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: The core facts F are a subset of the WorldTree corpus (Jansen et al., 2018), starting from 2287 facts marked as 'central' in at least one explanation, filtered down to 1326 general-purpose facts. Additional common knowledge sources used/referenced include ConceptNet, WordNet, Wikipedia, and a 14M science-related sentences corpus.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Answer choices were randomly shuffled to avoid unintended bias (since Choice 'A' was the correct answer in 69% of questions at end of Step 4).
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Basic checks included: exactly 4 answer choices; no negation words (to avoid trivially fooling baselines); uniform answer choice length (all with at most 3 or at least 4 words). Questions were filtered for hardness using an IR solver and a word association solver (neither should answer correctly and top 3 IR retrieved sentences should be insufficient). Questions not meeting the 4/5 crowd-worker answerability threshold were discarded (2,183 out of 8,140 collected were discarded).
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Crowd-workers authored each question: shown a random science fact f, asked to think of a second fact k, write a question-answer pair, and add 3 incorrect answer choices. A separate group of 5 crowd-workers answered each generated question to verify answerability (at least 4/5 correct required). Dev and Test questions were further reviewed by an in-house expert.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Human accuracy was estimated using a Bernoulli random variable model over the 5 answers per question from Step 6 of question generation. An application of Hoeffding's Inequality was used to derive confidence bounds; the conservative estimate of human performance is ~89.3% (Dev) and ~91.7% (Test). An additional 5 new annotations for 100 randomly chosen questions from each split yielded similar accuracy (88.6%, 90.2%, 91.6%).
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: 5 crowd-worker answers per question for answerability verification; additionally, Dev and Test questions received expert review.
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: Amazon Mechanical Turk workers from North America with 'masters' level qualification.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: IR solver (Clark et al., 2016) and word association based solver (Turney, 2017) were used during question generation to verify hardness.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The paper notes inevitable human bias in crowdsourced datasets. Simple neural baselines (plausible answer detector ignoring the question, odd-one-out solver) achieved ~50% accuracy, indicating bias in answer choices (e.g., incorrect answers tend to be homogeneous or share non-scientific properties). Choice 'A' was the correct answer in 69% of questions before shuffling. About 21% of questions test facts that do not actually require the original science fact.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The additional 'second facts' set K is noisy: often incomplete, over-complete, or only distantly related to the question; it should not be viewed as 'gold' additional facts. 21% of questions do not necessarily need the original science fact. Retrieval of the right common knowledge remains an open challenge. The dataset is limited to elementary-level science.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is split into 4,957 training, 500 development, and 500 test questions for training, validation, and testing of open book question answering systems. For each Train and Dev question, the associated fact f is included as intermediate supervision signal / partial explanation.
